title: Annotatio III §.X (6) cont.: Admits sign-accidents that must enter the substances; practical enmity — oral God-eating (Cicero / Averroes)
pass_a_gloss: Besides by admitting Species and Accidents of the Signs, bread and wine, of such a kind as nonetheless necessarily enter these signs’ substances — e.g. the bread’s quantity, from its defined Extension, and so not really diverse from the bread itself; the wine’s Motion in the Cup, least competent to bare Accidents i.e. emptied of all substantiality, yet seen in the subtler particles of wine held in the cup, which will exhale with time and by their flight diminish the wine’s substantial mass. But Transsubstantiation also threatens as enemy of Practical Philosophy when it also butts natural piety toward God and natural humanity. PIETY TOWARD GOD, by asserting God is eaten orally: Whom do you think so mad as to believe that what he feeds on is God? asks Cicero, De Natura Deorum bk. 3. To which answers Averroes’s judgment and sentence on Christianity: I have traversed all regions, and found no race worse than the Christian: Because the God they adore, they devour with their teeth. See Dionysius the Carthusian on 4 Dist. 10 Art. 1; compare Blessed Hottinger, Defense of the Eucharist pp. 214ff.
pass_b_english: It also admits bread/wine species that must enter those substances (bread’s quantity not really other than the bread; wine’s motion in the cup unfit for bare accidents, yet seen in exhalable particles that shrink the wine-mass).

Practical philosophy too: it butts natural piety — oral God-eating. Cicero: who is mad enough to think what he eats is God? Averroes: no worse race than Christians, who devour with teeth the God they adore (Hottinger pp. 214ff).
source_text: Prætereà Species & Accidentia Signorum, panis & vini, admittendo tales, quæ tamen signorum horum substantias necessariò ingrediuntur, e.g. Panis quantitatem ab Extensione ejus definita, ipsôque, adeo pane, realiter haud diversam; Vini Motum in Calice, Accidentibus nudis i. e. omni substantialitate orbis, minimè competentem, visum verò in subtilioribus vini, calice comprehensi, particulis, exhalaturis cum tempore, vinique massam substantialem, evolutione suâ imminuturis. Practica verò Philosophiæ inimica imminet Transsubstantiatio, quando etiam pietatem, in Deum, naturalem, & naturalem humanitatem arietat. PIETATEM IN DEUM, afferendo, Deum oraliter manducari: Ecquemnam tam amentem esse putas, qui id, quô vescitur, Deum esse credat? quærit Cicero de Natura Deorum Lib. 3. Cui respondet Averrois judicium sententiaque de Christianismo: Omnes regiones peragravi, nec Christianâ gente deteriorem ullam reperi: Quia quem Deum adorant, hunc dentibus devorant. vid. Dionys. Carthus. in 4. Dist. 10. Art. 1. Confer B. Hotting. Eucharist. defens. pag. 214. & seqq.
